'''Bakso''' or '''baso''' is an [[Indonesian Cuisine|Indonesian]] [[meatball]],<ref name="Rodgers">{{cite book | title = I Love Meatballs! | author = Rick Rodgers | publisher = Andrews McMeel Publishing| year = 2011 |isbn = 978-1-4494-1942-4 | page = 29 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=5EkNhZDpetwC&q=Bakso+Indonesian+meatballs&pg=PA29}}</ref> or a meat paste made from [[beef]] [[surimi]].<ref name="Nola">{{cite web |url=http://www.nola.com/politics/index.ssf/2010/11/bakso_the_soup_president_barac.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101208171510/http://www.nola.com/politics/index.ssf/2010/11/bakso_the_soup_president_barac.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 8, 2010 | title=Bakso: the soup President Barack Obama loved as a child | publisher=Nola.com article from The Associated Press}}</ref> Its texture is similar to the [[Chinese cuisine|Chinese]] [[beef ball]], [[fish ball]], or [[pork ball]]. The word ''bakso'' may refer to a single meatball or the complete dish of meatball soup. '''''[[Mie bakso]]''''' refers to bakso served with yellow noodles and rice vermicelli, while '''''bakso kuah''''' refers to bakso soup served without noodles.

''Bakso'' can be found all across Indonesia, from street vendors to high-class restaurants. Along with ''[[Soto (food)|soto]]'', ''[[satay]]'', and ''[[siomay]]'', ''bakso'' is one of the most popular [[street food]]s in Indonesia.<ref name="StreetFood">{{cite book | title = Street Food Around the World: An Encyclopedia of Food and Culture |author1=Bruce Kraig |author2=Colleen Taylor Sen | publisher = ABC-CLIO | year = 2013 | isbn = 978-1-59884-955-4| page = 182 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=9XCjAQAAQBAJ&q=Bakso+Indonesian+meatballs&pg=PA182}}</ref> Today, various types of ready-to-cook ''bakso'' are also available as [[frozen food]]s sold in [[supermarket]]s in Indonesia. It is usually eaten with noodles.
